description: 12th-grade physics and math student focused on astrophysics, orbital trajectories, and computational modeling. I handle the mathematical derivations, coordinate transformations, and physics engine logic behind our simulation.
summary:
ApsisEngine is a real-time 3D orbital mechanics and mission-planning simulation engine built from first principles. Rather than relying on pre-packaged physics libraries or black-box solvers, our engine translates raw Classical Orbital Elements into live orbital trajectories through rigorous mathematical modeling.
​To address the Space Mission Design Game challenge, ApsisEngine provides a transparent, data-driven environment where users can configure orbital parameters and instantly analyze how geometry and gravitational energy dictate spacecraft motion. Our computational pipeline integrates the Vis-Viva equation to evaluate continuous velocity variations between perigee and apogee, and deploys a Newton-Raphson iterative solver for Kepler’s transcendental equation to propagate true anomaly and time-of-flight accurately.  
​By grounding mission design in transparent vector mechanics rather than generic animations, ApsisEngine demonstrates how core mathematical physics governs authentic orbital trajectory planning.
details: ​We built ApsisEngine because we got tired of orbital simulators that treat physics like a black-box library you just import and ignore. Instead of letting pre-made game engines handle the math, we wanted to build a 3D trajectory simulator where every single pixel and calculation traces straight back to first-principles astrodynamics. ​How it works under the hood is pretty straightforward: you feed it raw orbital elements, and the engine runs the math line by line. We integrated the Vis-Viva equation so the code actually calculates how velocity scales as a satellite swings between perigee and apogee based on energy conservation. For the animation over time, true anomaly doesn't move linearly, so we wrote a Newton-Raphson iterative solver to crack Kepler's equation (M = E - e \sin E) so the time-of-flight stays accurate. ​We coded it using Python and NumPy, keeping things light since we focused our energy purely on the math and trajectory logic rather than heavy 3D rendering. ​We split the work cleanly between us: one person handled all the paper derivations, vector math, and numerical logic, while the other translated those equations into clean Python scripts and built the execution pipeline. It bridges the gap between raw physics and actual code without hiding anything behind fake animations.
